summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995. The operative instrument since 4 February 2010 is a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation across employment, goods and services, education, housing and health care; in October 2020 it was extended to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. On 4 May 2013 the Albanian Parliament amended the Criminal Code to place hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity on the same footing as offences rooted in race, ethnicity, religion or disability, and passed a law penalising the dissemination of homophobic information through any means, including the internet, by fine and up to two years' imprisonment.

Nothing in the record indicates trans-specific screening at the border or on arrival, and no restriction on facilities or bathrooms is on record. How documents are handled for visitors whose gender markers do not match their presentation is unresolved: the sources do not state whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists at all. In April 2018 People's Advocate Erinda Ballanca pledged to support the right to change one's gender legally, but the text does not record whether any procedure followed.

The realistic exposure is social rather than legal. Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people in 2023, and hostility is sharper outside Tirana and in more conservative rural areas. Gallup's Balkan Monitor found in 2010 that 56.1% of Albanians believed homosexual people should not show their preferences in public and 56.2% that they should not hold public posts such as teacher; a 2022 nationwide questionnaire found only 9.3% would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor, and 55% of Albanians aged 16 to 27 said in 2015 that they would not want homosexual neighbours.

International scrutiny is active. The UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, visited Albania from 1 to 12 July 2024, and report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 of 17 June 2025 evaluates the country's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on those grounds, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit. Tirana hosts an annual Pride, and a National LGBTI Action Plan runs from 2021 to 2027, with observers recording that implementation falls short of its commitments.
tangentialFactors:
Political rhetoric toward LGBT people is a live current in Albanian public life. In July 2021 Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a suspicious and revolting agenda, and in the same week MP Nard Ndoka posted on Facebook branding the government LGBT and accusing it of pushing LGBT values in schools.

Parliamentary hostility has an older record as well. On 27 October 2011 the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones, warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to earlier promises; PINK Embassy condemned the removal on 20 July 2016.

Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the issue as EU-integration driven, and the 2010 anti-discrimination law passed without a marriage provision. A 2016 study found homophobia among Albanian university students associated with being male, politically conservative and religious.
localsOnly:
The 2010 anti-discrimination law is enforced by the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination, but trust in the body among LGBT groups is low. Only one of nine LGBT-linked cases had concluded by December 2012, and investigations were described as slow and bureaucratically impeded. Tritan Shehu, then Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health, stated in December 2010 that homosexuality should be treated by medical staff as a hormonal and psychological disorder; the Commissioner reprimanded him only on 30 September 2011 after a lengthy delay.

Resident-facing support infrastructure exists despite weak state capacity. In 2023 groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV, and discrimination complaints filed over screenings of the film 'Strange World' were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour of complainants in one case.

A National Action Plan for LGBTI addressing bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education was passed by the government in June 2016 and drew strong political opposition; a further National LGBTI Action Plan covers 2021 to 2027. Visibility efforts by residents include the first Miss Trans Albania pageant in Tirana in 2014 and the news portal historiaime.al, launched by Pro LGBT in 2012.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists in Albania, and how Albanian authorities handle identity documents that do not match a person's presentation, remain unresolved. The record contains a 2018 pledge by the People's Advocate to support legal gender change but no source stating that a procedure was enacted or describing its requirements, and no source addressing document handling for arriving visitors.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules, border screening practices, or restrictions on restroom and facility use for trans visitors, so the absence of such findings should be read as not sourced rather than as a finding of permissiveness. Enforcement rates for the 2013 hate-crime provisions and the law penalising dissemination of homophobic information are also not sourced here; the inventory records the statutes' passage but no prosecutions under them.
